questions.prompt: Paragraph A
questions.evidence: Professional scribes, many of them working in monasteries and later in commercial workshops attached to universities, could spend months producing a single volume.

questions.evidence: What emerged there was less a single invention than a clever assembly of existing techniques.
questions.explanation: Paragraph B explains that printing combined casting, screw presses, paper and new ink. Cheap paper is only one part of this, so the heading about paper replacing parchment is too narrow.

questions.prompt: Paragraph C
questions.evidence: Yet printing was a risky business.
questions.explanation: Paragraph C describes how fast printing spread and how the risk of losing money made printers choose titles that would sell.

questions.prompt: Paragraph D
questions.evidence: Printing also altered the appearance and reliability of the book.
questions.explanation: Paragraph D covers new features such as title pages and indexes, and the double effect of printing on accuracy.

questions.prompt: Paragraph E
questions.evidence: Literacy in this period left few direct traces, and historians must rely on indirect evidence.
questions.explanation: Paragraph E reports a study of lists of possessions showing books appearing in craftsmen's homes, while warning that owning a book did not prove anyone could read it.

questions.prompt: Paragraph F
questions.evidence: the press amplified a demand for reading that already existed rather than creating one from nothing
questions.explanation: Paragraph F presents the view that printing strengthened an existing demand for reading but did not on its own create mass literacy.

questions.prompt: The printing system that appeared in Mainz around 1450 depended partly on paper, which by then cost much less than ______.
questions.evidence: had become far cheaper than parchment
questions.explanation: Paragraph B says paper had become far cheaper than parchment. 'Cost much less than' restates 'far cheaper than'.

questions.prompt: Letters were cast individually in metal and all given the same ______, which allowed them to be set in lines and used again.
questions.evidence: cast individual letters in metal, all of identical height
questions.explanation: Paragraph B says the metal letters were all of identical height, so they could be arranged into lines and reused.

questions.prompt: The water-based inks of the scribes were replaced by an ______ ink that stuck to the metal type more effectively.
questions.evidence: A new oil-based ink, which clung to metal better than the water-based inks used by scribes
questions.explanation: Paragraph B describes a new oil-based ink that 'clung to metal better', which the summary restates as 'stuck to the metal type more effectively'.

questions.prompt: Workers trained in Mainz carried the technique elsewhere, and by 1500 presses were operating in over ______ European towns.
questions.evidence: by 1500 printing presses had been set up in more than two hundred towns across Europe
questions.explanation: Paragraph C gives the figure of more than two hundred towns by 1500.

questions.prompt: ______ became one of the leading printing centres, helped by its rich merchants and its place on major trade routes.
questions.evidence: Venice, with its wealthy merchants and its position at the centre of trade routes, became one of the busiest centres
questions.explanation: Paragraph C names Venice as one of the busiest centres because of its wealthy merchants and its position on trade routes. Mainz is where printing began, not the city described here.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph A, why did two manuscripts of the same work often differ?

options.text: Mistakes made by one copyist were inherited by later copies.
Scribes in monasteries changed passages they disagreed with.
Parchment from different animals affected how words were written.
Universities and monasteries each preferred their own versions.

questions.evidence: Each scribe worked from an earlier copy, so a careless slip could be passed down and multiplied
questions.explanation: Paragraph A says each scribe copied from an earlier copy, so errors were passed down. Monasteries, universities and parchment are mentioned, but not as reasons why texts differed.

questions.prompt: What does the writer say about the effect of printing on accuracy?

options.text: It removed mistakes because printers checked every page.
It made errors far more common than in manuscripts.
It could preserve a correct text but also repeat a fault.
It quickly produced a single standard spelling everywhere.

questions.evidence: A carefully corrected text could be reproduced exactly, so scholars in different cities could at last discuss the same page. But an error that slipped past the printer appeared in every copy of the edition.
questions.explanation: Paragraph D describes a 'double effect': correct texts could be copied exactly, but an error appeared in every copy. The writer says full standardisation of spelling came much later, so the option about a quick single standard is wrong.

questions.prompt: What warning does Margit Hallström give about her findings?

options.text: Craftsmen bought religious books mainly to show off their wealth.
Having a book at home does not show that anyone there could read.
Most craftsmen could read but had never been taught to write.
Lists of possessions often leave out cheap books owned by families.

questions.evidence: Hallström cautions that owning a book did not prove that anyone in the household could read it.
questions.explanation: Paragraph E says Hallström warns that owning a book did not prove anyone in the household could read. The passage says 'many people' could read but not write; it does not say this was true of most craftsmen.

questions.prompt: What is Rashid Kalnins's main argument about the printing press?

options.text: It created an interest in reading among people who had none.
It made literacy rise quickly once presses reached most towns.
It mattered less than German pamphlets in spreading literacy.
It met a wish to read that was already present in society.

questions.evidence: the press amplified a demand for reading that already existed rather than creating one from nothing
questions.explanation: In paragraph F, Kalnins says the press strengthened a demand for reading that already existed. He says it did not create this demand, and that literacy rose slowly, so the options about creating interest and fast growth are wrong.

blocks.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

people.name: Margit Hallström
people.role: Historian who studied lists of possessions in sixteenth-century northern European towns

people.name: Rashid Kalnins
people.role: Economic historian who argues that printing amplified an existing demand for reading

paragraphs.text: Before the middle of the fifteenth century, every book in Europe had to be copied by hand. Professional scribes, many of them working in monasteries and later in commercial workshops attached to universities, could spend months producing a single volume. The materials added to the cost: much writing was done on parchment, prepared from animal skins, and a large book might require the skins of well over a hundred animals. As a result, books were valuable possessions, often chained to desks in libraries or listed alongside land and jewellery in wills. Copying also introduced mistakes. Each scribe worked from an earlier copy, so a careless slip could be passed down and multiplied, and two manuscripts of the same work rarely matched word for word. Readers who wanted to compare texts faced a genuine problem: they could not be sure they were reading the same words.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The change began in the German city of Mainz around 1450. What emerged there was less a single invention than a clever assembly of existing techniques. Metalworkers already knew how to cast objects in moulds; presses with a large screw were used to squeeze grapes and olives; and paper, which had reached Europe centuries earlier from the Islamic world, had become far cheaper than parchment. The decisive step was to cast individual letters in metal, all of identical height, so that they could be arranged into lines, locked into a frame, inked, printed and then taken apart and reused. A new oil-based ink, which clung to metal better than the water-based inks used by scribes, completed the system. A small team could now produce hundreds of identical pages in the time a scribe needed for a handful.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The method spread with remarkable speed. Workers trained in Mainz moved on to other cities, taking their skills with them, and by 1500 printing presses had been set up in more than two hundred towns across Europe. Venice, with its wealthy merchants and its position at the centre of trade routes, became one of the busiest centres of all. Yet printing was a risky business. A printer had to pay for metal, paper and labour long before a single copy was sold, and many early firms went bankrupt. To survive, printers chose titles they were confident would find buyers: prayer books, school grammars, calendars and legal handbooks. Far from being driven only by scholarly ideals, the early book trade followed the market.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Printing also altered the appearance and reliability of the book. Because buyers could now choose among competing editions in a shop, printers added features to attract and guide them. Title pages announced the content and often the place where copies could be purchased; page numbers and indexes allowed readers to find a passage quickly and to direct others to it. Smaller formats made books portable and cheaper. At the same time, the process had a double effect on accuracy. A carefully corrected text could be reproduced exactly, so scholars in different cities could at last discuss the same page. But an error that slipped past the printer appeared in every copy of the edition. Over time, the habits of influential printers also encouraged more consistent spelling, although full standardisation came much later.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Whether print made more people literate is harder to establish. Literacy in this period left few direct traces, and historians must rely on indirect evidence. One study by the historian Margit Hallström examined lists of possessions drawn up after deaths in several northern European towns during the sixteenth century. She found that books, rare in the homes of craftsmen at the start of the century, appeared in a growing share of them by its end, usually as one or two cheap religious titles. Hallström cautions that owning a book did not prove that anyone in the household could read it. Reading aloud was common, so a single literate family member might share a text with others, and many people who could read had never learned to write.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The economic historian Rashid Kalnins argues that the press amplified a demand for reading that already existed rather than creating one from nothing. Towns were growing, merchants needed records, and religious movements urged believers to read scripture in their own languages; printing allowed these pressures to be met on a scale that copying by hand never could. In the 1520s, for example, short pamphlets in German on religious questions were printed in huge numbers and passed from hand to hand. Even so, Kalnins notes, the proportion of Europeans who could read rose slowly, and in most regions it was the gradual expansion of schooling over the following centuries that turned reading into an everyday skill. The press, in his view, was a necessary condition for mass literacy but not a sufficient one.
paragraphs.label: F

section.text:
From Scribe to Press: How Printing Changed Reading

A. Before the middle of the fifteenth century, every book in Europe had to be copied by hand. Professional scribes, many of them working in monasteries and later in commercial workshops attached to universities, could spend months producing a single volume. The materials added to the cost: much writing was done on parchment, prepared from animal skins, and a large book might require the skins of well over a hundred animals. As a result, books were valuable possessions, often chained to desks in libraries or listed alongside land and jewellery in wills. Copying also introduced mistakes. Each scribe worked from an earlier copy, so a careless slip could be passed down and multiplied, and two manuscripts of the same work rarely matched word for word. Readers who wanted to compare texts faced a genuine problem: they could not be sure they were reading the same words.

B. The change began in the German city of Mainz around 1450. What emerged there was less a single invention than a clever assembly of existing techniques. Metalworkers already knew how to cast objects in moulds; presses with a large screw were used to squeeze grapes and olives; and paper, which had reached Europe centuries earlier from the Islamic world, had become far cheaper than parchment. The decisive step was to cast individual letters in metal, all of identical height, so that they could be arranged into lines, locked into a frame, inked, printed and then taken apart and reused. A new oil-based ink, which clung to metal better than the water-based inks used by scribes, completed the system. A small team could now produce hundreds of identical pages in the time a scribe needed for a handful.

C. The method spread with remarkable speed. Workers trained in Mainz moved on to other cities, taking their skills with them, and by 1500 printing presses had been set up in more than two hundred towns across Europe. Venice, with its wealthy merchants and its position at the centre of trade routes, became one of the busiest centres of all. Yet printing was a risky business. A printer had to pay for metal, paper and labour long before a single copy was sold, and many early firms went bankrupt. To survive, printers chose titles they were confident would find buyers: prayer books, school grammars, calendars and legal handbooks. Far from being driven only by scholarly ideals, the early book trade followed the market.

D. Printing also altered the appearance and reliability of the book. Because buyers could now choose among competing editions in a shop, printers added features to attract and guide them. Title pages announced the content and often the place where copies could be purchased; page numbers and indexes allowed readers to find a passage quickly and to direct others to it. Smaller formats made books portable and cheaper. At the same time, the process had a double effect on accuracy. A carefully corrected text could be reproduced exactly, so scholars in different cities could at last discuss the same page. But an error that slipped past the printer appeared in every copy of the edition. Over time, the habits of influential printers also encouraged more consistent spelling, although full standardisation came much later.

E. Whether print made more people literate is harder to establish. Literacy in this period left few direct traces, and historians must rely on indirect evidence. One study by the historian Margit Hallström examined lists of possessions drawn up after deaths in several northern European towns during the sixteenth century. She found that books, rare in the homes of craftsmen at the start of the century, appeared in a growing share of them by its end, usually as one or two cheap religious titles. Hallström cautions that owning a book did not prove that anyone in the household could read it. Reading aloud was common, so a single literate family member might share a text with others, and many people who could read had never learned to write.

F. The economic historian Rashid Kalnins argues that the press amplified a demand for reading that already existed rather than creating one from nothing. Towns were growing, merchants needed records, and religious movements urged believers to read scripture in their own languages; printing allowed these pressures to be met on a scale that copying by hand never could. In the 1520s, for example, short pamphlets in German on religious questions were printed in huge numbers and passed from hand to hand. Even so, Kalnins notes, the proportion of Europeans who could read rose slowly, and in most regions it was the gradual expansion of schooling over the following centuries that turned reading into an everyday skill. The press, in his view, was a necessary condition for mass literacy but not a sufficient one.

options.text: It quickly produced a single standard spelling everywhere.
It removed mistakes because printers checked every page.
It could preserve a correct text but also repeat a fault.
It made errors far more common than in manuscripts.

questions.prompt: What does the writer say about the effect of printing on accuracy?
questions.evidence: A carefully corrected text could be reproduced exactly, so scholars in different cities could at last discuss the same page. But an error that slipped past the printer appeared in every copy of the edition.

explanation.en: Paragraph D describes a 'double effect': correct texts could be copied exactly, but an error appeared in every copy. The writer says full standardisation of spelling came much later, so the option about a quick single standard is wrong.
explanation.ru: В абзаце D описан «double effect»: правильные тексты можно было воспроизводить точно, но ошибка попадала в каждый экземпляр. Автор пишет, что полная стандартизация орфографии наступила гораздо позже, поэтому вариант о быстром появлении единого стандарта неверен.
explanation.uk: В абзаці D описано «double effect»: правильні тексти можна було відтворювати точно, але помилка потрапляла в кожен примірник. Автор пише, що повна стандартизація правопису настала значно пізніше, тому варіант про швидку появу єдиного стандарту хибний.

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

options.text: Most craftsmen could read but had never been taught to write.
Craftsmen bought religious books mainly to show off their wealth.
Lists of possessions often leave out cheap books owned by families.
Having a book at home does not show that anyone there could read.

questions.prompt: What warning does Margit Hallström give about her findings?
questions.evidence: Hallström cautions that owning a book did not prove that anyone in the household could read it.

explanation.en: Paragraph E says Hallström warns that owning a book did not prove anyone in the household could read. The passage says 'many people' could read but not write; it does not say this was true of most craftsmen.
explanation.ru: В абзаце E сказано, что Hallström предупреждает: владение книгой не доказывало, что кто-либо в семье умел читать. В тексте говорится, что «many people» умели читать, но не писать; о том, что это относилось к большинству ремесленников, не сказано.
explanation.uk: В абзаці E сказано, що Hallström застерігає: володіння книжкою не доводило, що хтось у родині вмів читати. У тексті йдеться, що «many people» вміли читати, але не писати; про те, що це стосувалося більшості ремісників, не сказано.
